      Sugaring at home

      A cooked paste of sugar, lemon and water that rinses off. The main risk is burns, so test the heat every time.

      Ready to sugar today?

      Check anything that's true for the area you plan to sugar.

      Classic sugaring paste

      Ingredients
      • 1 cup (200 g) white sugar
      • 2 tbsp lemon juice, or ½ tsp citric acid plus 2 more tbsp water
      • 2 tbsp water
      Stovetop method
      1. Use a heavy, light-colored pot so you can see the color change.
      2. Stir everything over medium heat until the sugar dissolves.
      3. Once it boils, stop stirring. Swirl the pot gently and clip on a candy thermometer.
      4. Cook to 245–250°F (118–121°C), usually 8 to 12 minutes, until it's the color of honey or amber.
      5. Pour into a heat-safe glass jar. Keep children and pets away while it cools for 30 to 60 minutes, until warm and pliable.
      Reheating

      Take the lid off. Microwave in 5 to 10 second bursts and stir between them, since hot spots form in the middle. Test on your inner wrist before every use.

      Keeps: several months sealed at room temperature. Enough for about two lower legs.

      Cooking temperature

      Go by temperature, not time. Stove strength and batch size change how long it takes.

      No thermometer? Drop a little paste into a glass of cold water. At the right stage it forms a ball that holds its shape but flattens when you press it.

      How to sugar

      1. Exfoliate gently 1 to 2 days before, not the same day.
      2. Clean the skin and dry it completely. Dust lightly with cornstarch so the paste grips hair instead of skin.
      3. Test the paste on your inner wrist. It should feel warm like bathwater, never hot.
      4. Spread a thin layer against the direction of hair growth, going back and forth 2 or 3 times.
      5. Hold the skin taut and flick the paste off quickly, parallel to the skin, in the direction of hair growth.
      6. Go over the same spot no more than twice. Tweeze stray hairs instead.
      7. Rinse leftover sugar off with warm water. Don't put used paste back in the jar.

      Aftercare

      • For 24 to 48 hours: no sun or tanning, hot tubs, saunas, or long hot showers.
      • Skip workouts in tight clothing for a day. Sweat and friction irritate open follicles.
      • Skip fragranced lotion, and for underarms, deodorant, for a few hours.
      • Calm redness with a cool compress or plain aloe gel. Small red bumps usually fade within a day.
      • From day 3: exfoliate gently 2 or 3 times a week to prevent ingrown hairs.

      Fixing the paste

      • Runny, won't set: undercooked. Reheat and cook a few degrees higher.
      • Too hard to scoop: overcooked. Warm it with 1 tbsp water and stir.
      • Sticks to skin: paste too warm or skin damp. Let it cool and dust with cornstarch.
      • Won't grab hair: hair too short, or lotion on the skin. Wait a few days, or wash and dry the area.
      • Grainy or cloudy: the sugar crystallized. Reheat with a splash of water and lemon juice.

      If you get burned

      • Hold it under cool running water for 20 minutes. Don't use ice.
      • Don't peel stuck sugar off. Water dissolves it.
      • Cover loosely with a clean, non-stick dressing.
      • Get medical care for a burn larger than your palm, any blistering, or burns on the face, hands, feet, or genitals.

      Soap

      Enter your oils, lye and water. Superfat should land between 4 and 8%; below 0% leaves raw lye that burns.

      Recipe

      Oils and butters, in grams

      Uses typical saponification values. Oils vary a little from batch to batch, so confirm any recipe with a second lye calculator before you make it. Wear goggles and gloves, and always add lye to water. See "Before you make soap" on the Safety basics tab.

      Before you make soap

      • All real bar soap is made with lye (sodium hydroxide), including "natural" and "chemical-free" soap. A recipe that lists oils and herbs but no lye amount is incomplete, so don't follow it.
      • Lye causes severe burns and can blind. Wear goggles and gloves, work with ventilation, keep children and pets away, and always add lye to water, never water to lye.
      • Run every recipe through a lye calculator, and cure bars for 4 to 6 weeks before use.
      • Melt-and-pour soap base skips lye entirely. It's the safe way to start.
      • Selling soap: in Canada, cosmetics need a Health Canada notification within 10 days of the first sale and an ingredient list using INCI names. Claims like "treats acne" or "cures eczema" make it a drug, which has stricter rules.

      Traditional soaps compared

      Every true soap is alkaline (pH 9 to 10). The differences are in the oils, scent and texture, not in healing claims.

      SoapKey ingredientsGood atWatch for

      African black soap

      1
      Choose a blend
      2

      Batch size (grams of base)
      How to blend your own
      • Build in layers: about 30% top notes (citrus, herbs), 50% heart (florals, spice), 20% base (woods, vanilla, resins). Base notes last longest.
      • Mix the oils in a small glass bottle first, by drops, and let the blend sit 2 to 3 days before you judge it. Smell it on a paper strip, not straight from the bottle.
      • Many named flowers have no natural oil: freesia, lily of the valley, sweet pea, bluebell, lilac, peach, cherry and fig are all fragrance oils. Buy skin-safe fragrance oil from a soap supplier that lists its allergens and IFRA limits.
      • In anything that stays on skin, use bergamot FCF, never regular bergamot or cold-pressed lemon and lime, which can cause dark marks in the sun.
      • Strength depends on the product: rinse-off soap holds more scent than a powder, oil or balm that stays on skin all day.
      • Patch test any new blend on the inner arm for 48 hours, and keep strong spice oils (clove, cinnamon) out of leave-on blends.

      Routines

      Spa rituals at home, with the risky steps fixed. Tap one to open it.

      Hammam at home

      1. Steam or a hot shower, 5 to 10 minutes. Stop if you feel dizzy, and drink water.
      2. Black soap (savon beldi) on damp skin for 5 minutes. Keep it out of your eyes; it's alkaline.
      3. Kessa glove in firm, short strokes on the body. Grey rolls are dead skin. Stop at pink, not red, and go lightly or skip on the face, chest, and inner thighs.
      4. Rhassoul mask (optional), 5 to 10 minutes, then rinse.
      5. Argan oil or a plain moisturizer on damp skin.

      Once a week at most. Skip the glove on freshly shaved or waxed skin, sunburn, eczema patches, or while using retinoids.

      African black soap shower

      1. Lather the soap in your hands or on a cloth instead of rubbing the bar on skin. It's made with plant ash and can have sharp bits.
      2. Sapo net or loofah on the body, 2 or 3 times a week. Daily scrubbing is too much for most skin, and nets stay off the face.
      3. Body scrub (optional) on rough spots only, not on top of a net scrub.
      4. Rinse with lukewarm water.
      5. Shea butter or oil on damp skin.

      Black soap is strongly alkaline. If your skin feels tight or stings, use it less often. Hang nets to dry between uses, since damp nets grow mold.

      Pedicure and manicure at home

      1. Soak in warm (not hot) water with a little mild shampoo for 10 minutes. Skip the lemon slices; citrus on skin plus sun can leave dark marks.
      2. Scrub rough spots with sugar mixed with a little oil. Stir aloe or coffee in fresh each time rather than storing a wet scrub.
      3. Pack (optional): besan and yogurt for 10 minutes, then rinse. Turmeric tints nails and grout yellow.
      4. Push cuticles back gently after soaking. Don't cut them; they keep out infection.
      5. Moisturize with a cream or cuticle oil while skin is still damp.

      With diabetes or numb feet, check the water temperature with your hand or elbow and skip sharp tools.

      Bath teas and bath salts

      • Use fully dried herbs and put them in a muslin bag or infuser. Loose petals clog drains.
      • Warm, not hot: about 37 to 39°C (98 to 102°F) for 15 to 20 minutes. Hot baths dry skin and can make you lightheaded.
      • Mix essential oils into a carrier such as oil, unscented soap, or milk powder, and keep to about 12 drops per tub. Salt alone doesn't dissolve them.
      • Keep the jar dry. Add liquid milk or honey at bath time, not to the stored mix.
      • Oils make the tub slippery. Step out carefully and wipe the tub afterward.
      • For children: plain herbs and oats are fine from age 1; leave out essential oils, cayenne, and mustard.
      • Gift jars: list every ingredient on the tag so people can check for allergies.

      Banho de lua (body hair bleaching)

      A Brazilian treatment that lightens body hair to gold. It uses real bleach, so "chemical-free" versions with lemon and sun aren't safer: they risk burns and dark streaks.

      1. A day or two before: exfoliate gently. Don't bleach sunburned, broken, irritated, or freshly shaved or waxed skin.
      2. Choose a cream bleach kit made for body hair rather than salon powder. If using powder, 20 volume developer is the usual strength.
      3. Patch test 24 to 48 hours ahead: leave a small amount on for the full processing time, rinse, and wait.
      4. Apply to clean, dry skin with a brush, in sections, in an aired-out room. Use a plastic or glass bowl.
      5. Watch the time: follow the kit, never over 20 minutes. Rinse immediately if it burns.
      6. Rinse well with lukewarm water and mild soap. Skip the scrub today.
      7. Moisturize with a plain lotion or body oil, and keep out of the sun and tanning beds for 24 hours.

      Skip it during pregnancy, on eczema-prone skin, on the face or intimate areas, and for anyone under about 16.

      Skin icing

      • Wrap the cube in a thin cloth. Bare ice stuck to skin can cause ice burns.
      • Keep it moving, about 1 minute per area. Stop if skin turns white or numb.
      • Skip it with rosacea, broken capillaries, or broken skin, and before the face has warmed after being outside in the cold.
      • Freeze in a clean tray and use within a month. Turmeric and beet cubes stain.
      • The effect is temporary. Cold briefly reduces puffiness and redness; it doesn't shrink pores.

      Dry, cracked heels

      • Soak, then file gently with a foot file 1 or 2 times a week. Don't scrub open cracks.
      • Seal moisture in at night. Petroleum jelly or a urea foot cream under cotton socks is the most effective option, more than any oil.
      • Skip acids and baking soda on cracked skin. They sting and slow healing.
      • See a doctor for cracks that bleed, hurt to walk on, or look infected, and check feet daily if you have diabetes.

      Shop by need

      Choosing a clay gentlest to most drying

      All clays are rinse-off only: mix a fresh spoonful with water or hydrosol each time and rinse before it cracks.

      Clay absorbs oil and surface dirt. It doesn't pull "toxins" out of skin, and no clay disinfects or treats acne on its own. Don't use clay on sunburned or broken skin.

      Log a decision

      How Safe Batch judges a recipe

      No secret scores. Every verdict comes with the reasons behind it, so you can see exactly why and decide for yourself.

      How Safe Batch works

      How far does it get in?

      Skin has three layers. Most skincare works in the top one; only small, well-formulated molecules reach the second. That's why a 30-second cleanser can't "repair" anything, and why big molecules like collagen sit on the surface.

      EpidermisThe barrier. Renews every 4 to 6 weeks.
      Works hereOils and butters, humectants (glycerin, hyaluronic acid), cleansers, scrubs, collagen and most plant extracts
      DermisCollagen and elastin, made by fibroblasts.
      Small molecules reach the topRetinoids, vitamin C, niacinamide, AHAs and BHA, in well-made formulas over months
      HypodermisFat and cushioning.
      Needles, not creamsFillers, Botox and injected PDRN or growth factors are placed by a clinician

      Dose decides, not the name

      The same ingredient can be fine at 0.5% and harmful at 5%. Safe Batch works out the percentage of every ingredient and compares it with limits for that kind of product, such as essential oils at 1% on the face and 2% on the body.

      Three verdicts, never a number out of 100

      Ready to patch test, Adjust before using, or Don't use, each listing the exact problems. A single score hides why, and two different reasons can produce the same number.

      Natural isn't automatically safe. Synthetic isn't automatically harmful.

      Lemon juice and cinnamon oil can burn. Petroleum jelly is one of the gentlest, most protective things you can put on dry skin. Ingredients are judged on what they do, not where they come from.

      How you use it matters

      A mask rinsed off after 10 minutes is judged differently from a cream left on all day, the face differently from the feet, and a baby differently from an adult. Your profile changes the limits.

      Spoilage counts as much as irritation

      Water, aloe, tea or fresh food without a preservative grows mould and bacteria within days, often before you can see it. That's one of the most common reasons homemade recipes fail.

      Where the limits come from

      Widely used safety references: fragrance and essential oil limits like those in IFRA standards and essential oil safety texts, dermatology guidance, and published research. Viral claims are treated as claims to check, not facts.

      Where our facts come from

      Not every source counts the same. Safe Batch leans on the top tiers and treats the bottom ones as stories to check.

      1. Safety authoritiesPublished safety limits and official monographs (for example Tisserand and Young's essential oil limits, EU cosmetic rules, WHO and EMA plant monographs, Germany's Commission E).
      2. Human studiesTrials on people, ideally independent. Strongest when several agree.
      3. Lab and animal studiesUseful hints, but a cell in a dish isn't skin. We say "early evidence" when this is all there is.
      4. Tradition and practitionersCenturies of use tell us what people valued and what seemed safe; we keep the ritual and check the recipe.
      5. Brands and social postsClaims to test, not facts. Supplier test certificates (purity, heavy metals) are the exception and worth asking for.

      Ethical and eco labels, decoded

      These tell you how a product was made, not whether it suits your skin. Words like "clean", "conscious" or "responsibly made" on their own aren't certified; look for the mark.

      Leaping Bunny
      No animal testing anywhere in the supply chain, audited. The most reliable cruelty-free mark.
      Vegan (Vegan Society, V-Label)
      No animal-derived ingredients. Says nothing about testing or safety.
      COSMOS Organic or Ecocert
      A set share of organic ingredients and limits on processing. Organic doesn't mean gentler; essential oils are organic too.
      Fairtrade or Fair for Life
      Fair pay and safe conditions for the farmers and workers behind ingredients like shea and cocoa.
      B Corp
      The whole company is scored on social and environmental practices, not one product.
      FSC
      Paper and card packaging from responsibly managed forests.
      Cradle to Cradle
      Materials checked for safety, recyclability and renewable energy use.
      UPSM (Savon de Marseille)
      The French makers' union mark for authentic Marseille soap: at least 72% vegetable oils, cauldron-made.

      What Safe Batch can't do

      • Lab-test your actual batch, or know how fresh your ingredients are.
      • Know allergies you haven't added to your profile. Always patch test.
      • Diagnose or treat a skin condition. See a doctor for rashes that don't settle, eczema, or acne that hurts.

      Think a verdict is wrong? Use "Think this verdict is wrong?" under any result. Every report is read.

      Holistic, made safe

      Safe Batch doesn't pick a side. Tradition gives skincare its rituals and gentleness. Modern science gives it doses and proof. The checker sits in between.

      What we mean by holistic

      Traditional and whole-life care

      Plants, oils, butters, and rituals handed down through cultures, like Ayurvedic oiling, West African shea, the Moroccan hammam, and Chinese herbal care. It also looks past the skin itself, to sleep, food, stress, and sun.

      What we mean by modern

      Tested ingredients at known strengths

      Ingredients studied at a specific percentage, in products that are preserved and stability-tested. You'll find them in good drugstore, Korean and Japanese, pharmacy, and prescription products. It's not about a brand: price, packaging, and "clinically inspired" claims aren't evidence.

      Where they already meet

      K-beauty and J-beauty are a good example of the blend. Centella, ginseng, rice ferment, green tea, and mugwort are traditional herbs, sold as standardized extracts in preserved formulas. A DIY recipe can follow the same idea: keep the plant, and control the amount, the water, and the shelf life.

      How Safe Batch rates traditional practices

      Backed by evidence

      Good studies, or dermatology guidance, agree it works. Example: oat baths for itchy skin.

      Some evidence

      A small trial or a purified extract shows promise, so it's worth trying. Example: 5% tea tree gel for spots.

      Feels good, limited proof

      Safe and pleasant, but it doesn't do what the claim says. The ritual can still be worth keeping. Example: cocoa butter for stretch marks.

      Can backfire

      Likely to cause the problem it's meant to fix, or a new one. Example: lemon on dark spots.

      Where they agree

      • Be gentleFewer products, lukewarm water, no harsh scrubbing.
      • Seal moisture inShea, oils, and balms on damp skin are what moisturizers do too.
      • Look after the whole personSleep, stress, and diet show up on skin.
      • Stay out of the sunTraditional shade and covering up are the oldest anti-aging there is.

      Where they split

      • Dose"A few drops" quietly becomes 5% essential oil. Amounts matter.
      • SpoilageWater, aloe, and fresh food grow mould in days. Preservatives exist for this reason.
      • Real conditionsAcne, dandruff, hair loss, and dark spots respond far better to tested actives.
      • "Natural means safe"Lemon, baking soda, cinnamon, and garlic are natural, and some of the most common causes of harm.
      The rule of thumb

      Keep the ritual, check the recipe, and let tested ingredients treat the problem. Every goal has a "Holistic and modern, together" panel that shows what this looks like for that goal.

      By the numbers

      What the checker has found across every online DIY in Safe Batch, and in the recipes you've checked.

      Never put these on skin

      • Lemon or lime juice. Very acidic, and in sunlight it causes blistering burns and dark patches that can last months.
      • Baking soda. Strongly alkaline. It strips the skin's protective acid layer.
      • Undiluted essential oils. They can burn and cause a permanent allergy to that oil.
      • Black henna. It usually contains PPD, a hair dye chemical that causes blistering burns and a lifelong allergy to hair dye. Real henna is never black.
      • Traditional kohl (khol, kajal, surma). Many are made from lead sulfide, and lead poisoning in children has been traced to kohl. Use a regulated cosmetic eyeliner instead.
      • Raw garlic. Causes chemical burns, even in short contact.
      • Toothpaste, hydrogen peroxide, rubbing alcohol on spots. They damage healthy skin and slow healing.
      • Undiluted vinegar. Has caused chemical burns when left on skin.

      Clean kitchen habits

      • Wash hands, then wipe tools, bowls, and jars with 70% rubbing alcohol and let them air dry.
      • Use distilled or boiled-and-cooled water, never straight tap water.
      • Weigh ingredients on a scale in grams. Teaspoons vary a lot for powders and butters.
      • Make small batches. Label each jar with the name, ingredients, and the date you made it.
      • Scoop with a clean spoon instead of fingers. Throw out anything that changes smell, color, or texture.

      How to patch test

      1. Dab a coin-sized amount on your inner forearm or behind your ear.
      2. For leave-on products, leave it and don't wash the spot for 48 hours. For masks and scrubs, leave it on as long as you normally would, rinse, then watch for 48 hours.
      3. Redness, itching, burning, bumps, or swelling means don't use it. Wash the spot with plain water.
      4. Allergies can appear after several uses. Stop at the first sign of a reaction.

      Get medical help right away for blistering, facial or lip swelling, or trouble breathing.

      See a dermatologist instead when

      • You're treating acne that scars, eczema, psoriasis, rosacea, or a rash that won't clear.
      • A spot or mole is changing, bleeding, or not healing.
      • The product is for a baby under 1 year old.
      • You've had a reaction and don't know which ingredient caused it.
      Safe Batch uses conservative published guidance, including Tisserand & Young's essential oil safety limits. It can't test your batch, detect personal allergies, or replace a doctor or dermatologist. Don't sell or gift homemade products as if they were tested; commercial products go through stability and preservative testing that a home kitchen can't do.
